question: Six supplements, and the reason each is taken. For which reasons do trials say the pill does its job?
answer: The ones that work fill a gap someone really has. A baby forming a spine, a vegan with no animal foods, a breastfed infant: each lacks something specific. Healthy adults topping up a full tank get nothing measurable, which is why the big trials of fish oil and multivitamins came back flat.
move: Ask what gap a pill fills before asking whether it works.
ask: Which pill do I take without knowing what I am short of?

items.note: Taken while trying for a baby.
items.verdict: A 1991 trial cut spina bifida and similar defects by about 70%.

items.note: Taken by healthy adults to protect the heart.
items.verdict: In a trial of nearly 26,000 adults, heart attacks were no rarer than on dummy pills.
Plants do not make it. Without it, vegans risk anaemia and nerve damage.

items.note: One a day, to live longer.
items.verdict: In a trial of 14,000 doctors over a decade, takers died at the same rate.

items.note: Every day, to ward off colds.
items.verdict: Most people catch as many colds. Only those under extreme strain catch fewer.
Breast milk holds little of it. The drops prevent rickets: soft, bending bones.

source: MRC Vitamin Study, Lancet, 1991; VITAL, NEJM, 2019
reference: MRC Vitamin Study Research Group, Lancet 338:131-137, 1991; Manson et al., Marine n-3 fatty acids and prevention of cardiovascular disease and cancer, NEJM 380:23-32, 2019; Sesso et al., JAMA 308:1751-1760, 2012; Hemilä and Chalker, Vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold, Cochrane Database Syst Rev, 2013
